To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
protein-DNA binding is associated with SMs in diverse cancers.
protein binding and open regions are enriched in the vicinity of structural mutation (SM) breakpoints in diverse cancers.
protein binding and open (accessible) chromatin are associated with SM breakpoints across diverse cancer types.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between chromatin features and SMs in cancer and provides a comprehensive analysis of this relationship across multiple cancer datasets.
the relationship among SMs, chromatin state and protein binding in diverse cancers.
the role of chromatin structure in cancer and its relationship with SMs, which are a major driver of cancer development.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

SMs are not random, and that they are not only associated with open chromatin and protein-DNA binding, but that they also occur more frequently in regions distant from transcriptional units, suggesting that the mechanism inducing SMs is independent from DSBs occurring near transcribed regions.
SMs are not random, but are associated with protein binding and open regions of chromatin, which may be a common mechanism across different cancers.
the SM-inducing mechanism is independent of the bias of DMBs to occur near genes, but is dependent on the binding of multiple proteins.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
SM breakpoints are enriched near protein binding sites and open chromatin, but not in regions of high gene expression.

protein-DNA interactions are associated with SM breakpoints, but that the mechanism underlying the bias of SMs to occur in active chromatin is distinct from that underlying DSB bias to occur in transcribed regions.
SMs are not randomly distributed, but rather are associated with functional features of the genome, such as protein binding and chromatin state.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the SM-inducing mechanisms are not limited to a few cancers and that they are likely to be general across different cancer types.
protein-DNA binding and open chromatins are important factors in SM formation.
the chromatin state in the vicinity of the DSB is an important determinant of SM location.
